summary: The Debt calculator works out total debt from the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1, the interest rate #2 and the payment #1. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Debt calculator work?
sections.html:
The Debt calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total debt in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of debts); then you type in the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 6), the interest rate boxes (numbered 1 to 7), the payment boxes (numbered 1 to 6) and the prepaid fee.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Debt calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total debt=(balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, number of debts)
Monthly payment=(payment #1, payment #2, payment #3, payment #4, payment #5, payment #6, number of debts)
Debt apr=(number of debts, balance #1, interest rate #1, payment #1, balance #2, interest rate #2, payment #2, balance #3, interest rate #3, payment #3, balance #4, interest rate #4, payment #4, balance #5, interest rate #5, payment #5, balance #6, interest rate #6, payment #6, interest rate, prepaid fee)
Min interest=((number of debts, balance #1, interest rate #1, payment #1, balance #2, interest rate #2, payment #2, balance #3, interest rate #3, payment #3, balance #4, interest rate #4, payment #4, balance #5, interest rate #5, payment #5, balance #6, interest rate #6, payment #6, interest rate, prepaid fee))
Min payoff after=((number of debts, balance #1, interest rate #1, payment #1, balance #2, interest rate #2, payment #2, balance #3, interest rate #3, payment #3, balance #4, interest rate #4, payment #4, balance #5, interest rate #5, payment #5, balance #6, interest rate #6, payment #6, interest rate, prepaid fee))
Snowball apr=((number of debts, balance #1, interest rate #1, payment #1, balance #2, interest rate #2, payment #2, balance #3, interest rate #3, payment #3, balance #4, interest rate #4, payment #4, balance #5, interest rate #5, payment #5, balance #6, interest rate #6, payment #6, interest rate, prepaid fee))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Balance #1: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Interest rate #1: %, opening in percent
  • Payment #1: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Balance #2: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Interest rate #2: %, opening in percent
  • Payment #2: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Balance #3: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Interest rate #3: %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Debt calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1 and the interest rate #2 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Debt calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total debt, derived from the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1 and the interest rate #2. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Debt calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1, the interest rate #2 and the payment #1, which is 34 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter balance #1 in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Balance #1 opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Debt calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
